questions.q: Which of the following events laid the foundation of central administration in India?
questions.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step taken by the British Government to control and regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India and laid the foundations of central administration.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Regulating Act of 1773: 1️⃣ It designated the Governor of Bengal as the ‘Governor-General of India’. 2️⃣ It created an Executive Council of four members to assist him. 3️⃣ Lord Warren Hastings was the first such Governor-General.
questions.e: The Act designated the Governor of Bengal as the ‘Governor-General of Bengal’, not India. Lord Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General, assisted by a four-member Executive Council.

questions.q: With reference to the Supreme Court established under the Regulating Act of 1773, consider the following: 1️⃣ It was established at Calcutta in 1774. 2️⃣ It comprised one chief justice and three other judges. 3️⃣ It had jurisdiction over all the inhabitants of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
questions.e: The Supreme Court was established at Calcutta in 1774 with one chief justice and three other judges. The Amending Act of 1781 later specified its jurisdiction over the inhabitants of Calcutta.

questions.q: Which act is also known as the ‘Act of Settlement’?
questions.e: The British Parliament passed the Amending Act of 1781 to rectify the defects of the Regulating Act of 1773; it is also known as the Act of Settlement.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Amending Act of 1781: 1️⃣ It exempted the Governor-General and Council from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court for official acts. 2️⃣ It required the Court to administer the personal law of the defendants. 3️⃣ Appeals from Provincial Courts were to be taken to the Supreme Court.
questions.e: The Act exempted the Governor-General and Council from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for official actions and required Hindu/Mohammedan personal laws to be applied. Appeals from Provincial Courts went to the Governor-General-in-Council, not the Supreme Court.

questions.q: Which of the following acts established a system of ‘double government’ in British India?
questions.e: Pitt’s India Act of 1784 distinguished between commercial and political functions, allowing the Court of Directors to manage commerce while creating a Board of Control for political affairs.

questions.q: Under which act were the Company’s territories in India called the ‘British possessions in India’ for the first time?
questions.e: Pitt’s India Act of 1784 was significant because the Company's territories were first called 'British possessions in India' and the British Government was given supreme control over administration.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Lord Cornwallis: 1️⃣ He was appointed as the Governor-General of Bengal in 1786. 2️⃣ He demanded the power to override his council in special cases. 3️⃣ He was the first Governor-General to be also the Commander-in-Chief.
questions.e: Lord Cornwallis was appointed in 1786 and accepted the post on two conditions: the power to override his council and being the Commander-in-Chief. The Act of 1786 enacted these provisions.

questions.q: Which act extended the trade monopoly of the East India Company for a period of another twenty years?
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the trade monopoly of the Company in India for a period of another twenty years.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1813: 1️⃣ It abolished the trade monopoly of the Company in India completely. 2️⃣ It allowed Christian missionaries to come to India. 3️⃣ It provided for the spread of western education in British territories.
questions.e: The Act abolished the trade monopoly except for trade in tea and trade with China. It also allowed Christian missionaries and provided for the spread of western education.

questions.q: Which act was the ‘final step’ towards centralisation in British India?
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1833 was the final step towards centralisation in British India as it made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India with all civil and military powers.

questions.q: Who was the first Governor-General of India?
questions.e: Lord William Bentick was the first Governor-General of India, vested with authority over the entire territorial area possessed by the British in India.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1833: 1️⃣ It ended the activities of the East India Company as a commercial body. 2️⃣ It introduced a successful system of open competition for the selection of civil servants. 3️⃣ It deprived the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers.
questions.e: The Act ended the Company’s commercial activities and deprived Bombay and Madras of legislative powers. However, the attempt to introduce open competition for civil servants was negated due to opposition from the Court of Directors.

questions.q: Which act established a separate ‘Indian (Central) Legislative Council’?
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s council and established the Indian (Central) Legislative Council.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1853: 1️⃣ It introduced local representation in the Indian Legislative Council. 2️⃣ Four members were appointed by the local governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal, and Agra. 3️⃣ It threw open the covenanted civil service to Indians.
questions.e: The Act introduced local representation (4 out of 6 members from specific provinces) and threw open the covenanted civil service to Indians, leading to the appointment of the Macaulay Committee.

questions.q: Which act is known as the ‘Act for the Good Government of India’?
questions.e: The Government of India Act of 1858, enacted in the wake of the 1857 Revolt, was known as the Act for the Good Government of India; it abolished the East India Company.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India Act of 1858: 1️⃣ It changed the designation of Governor-General of India to Viceroy of India. 2️⃣ Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India. 3️⃣ It created the office of Secretary of State for India responsible to the British Parliament.
questions.e: The Act made the Governor-General the Viceroy (Canning being the first) and created the Secretary of State for India, a British Cabinet member responsible to the British Parliament.

questions.q: Which of the following bodies were abolished by the Government of India Act of 1858? 1️⃣ Board of Control 2️⃣ Court of Directors 3️⃣ Council of India
questions.e: The Act of 1858 ended the system of double government by abolishing the Board of Control and the Court of Directors. The Council of India was actually established by this act to assist the Secretary of State.

questions.q: Which act restored the legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, initiating decentralisation?
questions.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 initiated the process of decentralisation by restoring legislative powers to Bombay and Madras, reversing the trend started in 1773.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Councils Act of 1861: 1️⃣ It introduced the ‘portfolio’ system. 2️⃣ It empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances during an emergency. 3️⃣ It provided for the nomination of Indians as non-official members to the legislative council.
questions.e: The Act associated Indians with law-making (nominating three in 1862), recognised the portfolio system (introduced in 1859), and empowered the Viceroy to issue 6-month ordinances.

questions.q: Which act gave the legislative councils the power of discussing the budget and addressing questions to the executive?
questions.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 increased the functions of legislative councils, giving them the power to discuss the budget and question the executive.

questions.q: Which act is also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms?
questions.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, named after Secretary of State Lord Morley and Viceroy Lord Minto.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Councils Act of 1909: 1️⃣ It increased the size of the Central Legislative Council from 16 to 60. 2️⃣ It provided for the first time for the association of Indians with the executive councils of the Viceroy. 3️⃣ Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian Law Member.
questions.e: The Act raised council membership to 60 and allowed Indians in executive councils; Satyendra Prasad Sinha was the first Indian to join the Viceroy’s executive council as Law Member.

questions.q: Who is known as the ‘Father of Communal Electorate’?
questions.e: Lord Minto is known as the Father of Communal Electorate because the Indian Councils Act of 1909 introduced a system of communal representation for Muslims through separate electorates.

questions.q: Which act is also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms?
questions.e: The Government of India Act of 1919 is also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, named after Secretary of State Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India Act of 1919: 1️⃣ It introduced ‘dyarchy’ in the provinces. 2️⃣ It introduced bicameralism and direct elections in the country for the first time. 3️⃣ It separated the provincial budgets from the Central budget.
questions.e: The Act introduced dyarchy (transferred and reserved subjects), established a bicameral legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly), and separated provincial budgets from the central one.

questions.q: Under the Government of India Act of 1919, which of the following subjects were categorized as ‘Transferred’?
questions.e: Transferred subjects included public health, education, local self-government, and agriculture, administered by the Governor with Ministers. Reserved subjects included police, justice, and land revenue.

questions.q: When was the Central Public Service Commission set up for recruiting civil servants?
questions.e: The Government of India Act of 1919 provided for the establishment of a public service commission; hence, the Central Public Service Commission was set up in 1926.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Simon Commission: 1️⃣ It was a seven-member statutory commission appointed in 1927. 2️⃣ All its members were British, leading to a boycott by all parties. 3️⃣ It recommended the abolition of dyarchy and continuation of communal electorates.
questions.e: Appointed in 1927 under Sir John Simon, the commission was boycotted because all members were British. It recommended abolishing dyarchy and continuing communal electorates.

questions.q: The ‘Poona Pact’ of 1932 resulted in:
o: Reserved seats for depressed classes in joint electorates
Creation of a separate state for Sikhs
questions.e: Distressed by separate electorates for depressed classes in the Communal Award, Gandhiji fasted; the resulting Poona Pact retained Hindu joint electorates and gave reserved seats to depressed classes.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India Act of 1935: 1️⃣ It provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation. 2️⃣ It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced ‘provincial autonomy’. 3️⃣ It provided for the adoption of dyarchy at the Centre.
questions.e: The Act proposed a federation (which never formed), replaced provincial dyarchy with autonomy, and provided for dyarchy at the Centre (though this did not operate).

questions.q: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, the Federal List for the Centre contained how many items?
questions.e: The Act divided powers into three lists: Federal List (Centre, 59 items), Provincial List (Provinces, 54 items), and Concurrent List (Both, 36 items).

questions.q: Which of the following institutions were established under the Government of India Act of 1935? 1️⃣ Reserve Bank of India 2️⃣ Federal Court 3️⃣ Provincial Public Service Commissions
questions.e: The Act provided for the Reserve Bank of India (1935), a Federal Court (1937), and Public Service Commissions at Federal, Provincial, and Joint levels.

questions.q: On which date did the British Prime Minister Clement Atlee declare that British rule in India would end?
questions.e: On February 20, 1947, Clement Atlee declared British rule would end by June 30, 1948, transferring power to responsible Indian hands.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Independence Act of 1947: 1️⃣ It abolished the office of Viceroy. 2️⃣ It abolished the office of Secretary of State for India. 3️⃣ It proclaimed the lapse of British paramountcy over princely states.
questions.e: The Act abolished the Viceroy (providing Governors-General instead) and the Secretary of State, and proclaimed the lapse of British paramountcy from August 15, 1947.

questions.q: Who was the first Governor-General of the new Dominion of India?
questions.e: Lord Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of the new Dominion of India and swore in Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister.

questions.q: Match the following members of the Interim Government (1946) with their portfolios: 1️⃣ Sardar Patel: Home 2️⃣ Dr. Rajendra Prasad: Food and Agriculture 3️⃣ Jagjivan Ram: Labour
o: All three pairs are correctly matched
Only two pairs are correctly matched
Only one pair is correctly matched
None of the pairs are correctly matched
questions.e: In the 1946 Interim Government, Sardar Patel held Home, Information and Broadcasting; Dr. Rajendra Prasad held Food and Agriculture; and Jagjivan Ram held Labour.

questions.q: Who held the portfolio of Law in the First Cabinet of Independent India (1947)?
questions.e: In the first cabinet of independent India, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Law Minister. Jogendra Nath Mandal held Law in the 1946 Interim Government.

questions.q: Who put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India for the first time in 1934?
questions.e: The idea of a Constituent Assembly for India was put forward for the first time in 1934 by M.N. Roy, a pioneer of the communist movement.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the demand for a Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ The INC officially demanded it for the first time in 1935. 2️⃣ The demand was accepted in principle by the British in the ‘August Offer’ of 1940. 3️⃣ The Muslim League accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan.
questions.e: INC demanded it in 1935, and the British accepted it in the 1940 August Offer. While the Muslim League rejected the 1942 Cripps Proposals, it was "more or less satisfied" by the Cabinet Mission Plan.

questions.q: What was the total strength of the Constituent Assembly as per the Cabinet Mission Plan?
questions.e: The total strength of the Constituent Assembly was to be 389, with 296 seats for British India and 93 seats for princely states.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding seat allocation in the Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ Seats were allotted in proportion to the respective population. 2️⃣ Roughly, one seat was allotted for every million population. 3️⃣ Princely states were to be represented by elected members.
questions.e: Seats were proportional to population (1 per million). Representatives of British provinces were elected community-wise, but representatives of princely states were nominated by their heads.

questions.q: The elections to the Constituent Assembly in July-August 1946 resulted in the INC winning how many seats?
questions.e: Out of the 296 seats allotted to British Indian Provinces, the Indian National Congress won 208 seats, while the Muslim League won 73.

questions.q: Who was elected as the temporary Chairman of the Constituent Assembly in its first meeting?
questions.e: The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on December 9, 1946. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was elected as the temporary Chairman.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the ‘Objectives Resolution’: 1️⃣ It was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946. 2️⃣ It was adopted by the Assembly on January 22, 1947. 3️⃣ Its modified version forms the Preamble of the present Constitution.
questions.e: Nehru moved the historic resolution in 1946, which was adopted in 1947 and eventually shaped the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.

questions.q: Which act made the Constituent Assembly a fully sovereign body and also a legislative body?
questions.e: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 made the Assembly a sovereign body that could abrogate British laws and assigned it two functions: making the constitution and enacting ordinary laws.

questions.q: Who chaired the Constituent Assembly when it met as a legislative body?
questions.e: When the Assembly met as a constituent body, it was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad; when it met as a legislative body, it was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar.

questions.q: What was the final strength of the Constituent Assembly for India after the withdrawal of Muslim League members from Pakistan areas?
questions.e: Following the partition, the total strength of the Assembly came down to 299 from 389, with Indian province seats reduced to 229 and princely state seats to 70.

questions.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly adopt the national flag?
questions.e: The Constituent Assembly adopted the national flag on July 22, 1947. The national anthem, national song, and the first President were adopted/elected on January 24, 1950.

questions.q: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the most important committee, the Drafting Committee, set up on August 29, 1947.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of Constituent Assembly committees and chairmen: 1️⃣ Union Powers Committee: Jawaharlal Nehru 2️⃣ Provincial Constitution Committee: Sardar Patel 3️⃣ Steering Committee: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
o: Only one pair is correctly matched
None of the pairs are correctly matched
Only two pairs are correctly matched
All three pairs are correctly matched
questions.e: Nehru chaired the Union Powers and Union Constitution committees; Sardar Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution and Advisory committees; and Dr. Rajendra Prasad chaired the Steering and Rules of Procedure committees.

questions.q: How many sessions did the Constituent Assembly have in total to frame the Constitution?
questions.e: In all, the Constituent Assembly had 11 sessions over two years, 11 months, and 18 days to complete the task of making the Constitution.

questions.q: Which date is mentioned in the Preamble as the date on which the people of India adopted the Constitution?
questions.e: The motion on the Draft Constitution was declared passed on November 26, 1949; this is the date mentioned in the Preamble as the date of adoption and enactment.

questions.q: Why was January 26 specifically chosen as the ‘date of commencement’ of the Constitution?
o: It was the date of the First War of Independence.
It was the date the Drafting Committee was formed.
It was the date Purna Swaraj day was celebrated in 1930.
It was the date of the Quit India Movement.
questions.e: January 26 was chosen because it was on this day in 1930 that Purna Swaraj day was celebrated following the Lahore Session resolution of the INC.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the criticism of the Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ Critics called it a ‘Drifting Committee’ due to the time consumed. 2️⃣ Granville Austin remarked that the Assembly was the Congress and the Congress was India. 3️⃣ Winston Churchill commented that it represented only one major community in India.
questions.e: Critics claimed the Assembly was non-representative, time-consuming (Naziruddin Ahmed coined ‘Drifting Committee’), and dominated by the Congress and Hindus.

questions.q: Who was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor (Legal Advisor) to the Constituent Assembly?
questions.e: Sir B.N. Rau was appointed as the constitutional advisor, while H.V.R. Iyengar was the Secretary and S.N. Mukherjee was the chief draftsman.

questions.q: Which animal was adopted as the symbol (seal) of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.e: The elephant was adopted as the symbol (seal) of the Constituent Assembly.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Hindi version of the Constitution: 1️⃣ The original Constitution made no provision for an authoritative Hindi text. 2️⃣ The 58th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1987 provided for an authoritative text in Hindi. 3️⃣ Vasant Krishan Vaidya did the calligraphy of the Hindi version.
questions.e: Initially there was no provision; Article 394-A was inserted in 1987. Vasant Krishan Vaidya was the calligrapher for the Hindi version, decorated by Nand Lal Bose.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a quality of a good constitution as per the concept of the constitution?
questions.e: A good constitution should have qualities like brevity, clarity, definiteness, comprehensiveness, suitability, and stability. It should be dynamic (adaptable), not static.

questions.q: On the basis of evolution, the British Constitution is an example of:
questions.e: An evolved (cumulative) constitution is the outcome of a slow process (conventions, practices); the British Constitution is a prime example. American and Indian constitutions are enacted.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding ‘Constitutionalism’: 1️⃣ It connotes essentially limited government. 2️⃣ It is the antithesis of arbitrary power. 3️⃣ A country with a constitution always has constitutionalism.
questions.e: Constitutionalism means limited government and rule of law. A country may have a constitution but not constitutionalism (e.g., a dictatorship).

questions.q: Who identified the eight elements of constitutionalism, including popular sovereignty and rule of law?
questions.e: Constitutional scholar Louis Henkin identified eight elements, such as popular sovereignty, rule of law, separation of powers, and an independent judiciary.

questions.q: Which amendment act is known as the ‘Mini-Constitution’?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) is known as the 'Mini-Constitution' because of the large number of substantial changes it made to various parts of the Constitution.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the salient features of the Indian Constitution: 1️⃣ It is the lengthiest written constitution in the world. 2️⃣ It is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility. 3️⃣ It provides for a federal system with a unitary bias.
questions.e: India’s constitution is uniquely long, combines special and simple amendment procedures, and features a dual polity but with a strong Centre.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-federal or unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
questions.e: Federal features include two governments, division of powers, and bicameralism. Unitary features include a strong Centre, single Constitution, and single citizenship.

questions.q: The ‘Procedure established by Law’ in Article 21 is borrowed from which constitution?
questions.e: The Indian Constitution’s ‘Procedure established by Law’ is drawn from the Japanese Constitution, differing from the American ‘due process of law’.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Preamble: 1️⃣ It is based on the ‘Objectives Resolution’ moved by Nehru. 2️⃣ It has been amended twice so far. 3️⃣ The 42nd Amendment Act added the words ‘Socialist, Secular and Integrity’.
questions.e: The Preamble is based on Nehru’s resolution. It has been amended only once (1976), adding ‘Socialist’, ‘Secular’, and ‘Integrity’.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution?
questions.e: In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Court said Preamble is NOT a part. This was rejected in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), which held it IS a part.

questions.q: Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as a:
questions.e: Article 1 describes India as a ‘Union of States’, signifying that the federation is not a result of an agreement and states have no right to secede.

questions.q: Which article empowers the Parliament to form new states and alter areas, boundaries, or names of existing states?
questions.e: Article 2 relates to admitting/establishing NEW states (not part of the Union). Article 3 deals with changes to EXISTING constituent states.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding state reorganisation: 1️⃣ A bill for altering state boundaries needs prior recommendation of the President. 2️⃣ The Parliament is bound by the views of the state legislature. 3️⃣ India is described as ‘an indestructible union of destructible states’.
questions.e: Prior presidential recommendation is needed, but the Parliament is not bound by the state’s views. Thus, India can redraw its map, unlike the USA.

questions.q: Which was the first linguistic state created in India?
questions.e: In October 1953, the government was forced to create Andhra state by separating Telugu-speaking areas from Madras state following Potti Sriramulu's death.

questions.q: The Dhar Commission (1948) recommended the reorganisation of states on the basis of:
questions.e: The Linguistic Provinces Commission under S.K. Dhar recommended reorganisation based on administrative convenience rather than linguistic factors.

questions.q: Which constitutional amendment act conferred on Sikkim the status of an ‘associate state’?
questions.e: The 35th Amendment (1974) made Sikkim an ‘associate state’. The 36th Amendment (1975) later made it a full-fledged 22nd state.

questions.q: Which of the following fundamental rights are available ONLY to citizens of India?
o: Protection of language, script and culture of minorities (Article 29)
Protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21)
questions.e: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are available only to citizens. Other rights like 14, 20, 21, and 25 are available to both citizens and foreigners.

questions.q: Which article defines the ‘State’ for the purposes of Fundamental Rights?
questions.e: Article 12 defines the ‘State’ to include the Union and State governments/legislatures, local authorities, and other statutory bodies.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Article 13: 1️⃣ It expressively provides for the doctrine of judicial review. 2️⃣ It declares that a constitutional amendment is not a law. 3️⃣ The Supreme Court held that amendments can be challenged if they violate the ‘basic structure’.
questions.e: Article 13 makes laws void if they contravene FRs. While it says amendments aren't 'laws', the Kesavananda case allows challenging them on 'basic structure' grounds.

questions.q: ‘Rule of Law’ as propounded by A.V. Dicey includes: 1️⃣ Absence of arbitrary power. 2️⃣ Equality before the law. 3️⃣ The constitution is the source of individual rights.
questions.e: Dicey's first two elements apply to India. The third (rights from court decisions rather than a constitution) does not, as the Indian constitution is the source of rights.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution provides for the reservation of up to 10% of seats for Economically Weaker Sections (EWSs) in educational institutions?
questions.e: Article 15(6) was added by the 103rd Amendment Act, 2019, allowing up to 10% reservation for EWS in educational institutions (including private ones).

questions.q: The ‘creamy layer’ exclusion principle for OBCs was directed by the Supreme Court in:
questions.e: In the Indra Sawhney case, the Court upheld 27% OBC reservation but directed the government to exclude the advanced 'creamy layer' from benefits.

questions.q: Which article abolishes ‘untouchability’ and forbids its practice?
questions.e: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence punishable by law.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Article 19: 1️⃣ It guarantees seven rights to all citizens. 2️⃣ These rights are protected against only state action. 3️⃣ The state can impose ‘reasonable’ restrictions on specific grounds.
questions.e: Article 19 now guarantees six rights (property was deleted in 1978). They are protected only against state action and subject to reasonable restrictions.

questions.q: Which case introduced the ‘due process of law’ expression into the interpretation of Article 21?
questions.e: In the Maneka case, the Court overruled the narrow Gopalan interpretation, requiring procedures to be fair and just, effectively introducing 'due process of law'.

questions.q: The Right to Education (Article 21A) was added by which amendment?
questions.e: The 86th Amendment Act of 2002 made elementary education (age 6 to 14) a fundamental right under Article 21A.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention: 1️⃣ No democratic country has it as an integral part of its constitution except India. 2️⃣ It can exceed three months only if an advisory board finds sufficient cause. 3️⃣ The 44th Amendment reduced this period to two months, and it is currently in force.
questions.e: India is unique in constitutionalizing preventive detention. The 3-month limit requires an advisory board for extension. The 44th Amendment's reduction to 2 months hasn't been brought into force.

questions.q: Which writ is issued by the court to enquire into the legality of a claim of a person to a public office?
questions.e: Quo-Warranto (by what authority) is issued to prevent illegal usurpation of a permanent substantive public office.

questions.q: Directive Principles of State Policy are enumerated in:
questions.e: DPSP are enumerated in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36 to 51), while Fundamental Rights are in Part III.

questions.q: Who described the Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights as the ‘Conscience of the Constitution’?
questions.e: Granville Austin described DPSP and Fundamental Rights as the 'Conscience of the Constitution'. Ambedkar described DPSP as 'novel features'.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding DPSP: 1️⃣ They are legally enforceable by the courts. 2️⃣ They are fundamental in the governance of the country. 3️⃣ They aim at establishing social and economic democracy.
questions.e: DPSP are non-justiciable (not legally enforceable) but are fundamental in governance and aim for social and economic democracy.

questions.q: Which article directs the State to organise village panchayats?
questions.e: Article 40 (a Gandhian Principle) requires the State to organise village panchayats and endow them with powers of self-government.

questions.q: The Fundamental Duties were added on the recommendation of:
questions.e: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976) based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

questions.q: How many Fundamental Duties were initially added by the 42nd Amendment Act?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 10 duties. An 11th duty (education for children 6-14) was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Fundamental Duties: 1️⃣ They are applicable to both citizens and foreigners. 2️⃣ They are non-justiciable in nature. 3️⃣ The Verma Committee (1999) identified existing legal provisions for some duties.
questions.e: Fundamental Duties are confined to citizens only. They are non-justiciable, but legal provisions (like the Flag Code/Penal Code) enforce some aspects.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A?
questions.e: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended a duty to pay taxes, but it was not accepted or incorporated into the Constitution.

questions.q: In case of conflict between Fundamental Rights and DPSP, the current position is:
o: They are both equally enforceable in courts.
Fundamental Rights enjoy supremacy, but can be amended for DPSP.
questions.e: The Supreme Court holds that FRs enjoy supremacy, but Parliament can amend them to implement DPSP as long as the 'basic structure' is not damaged.

questions.q: Which case held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of balance between FRs and DPSP?
questions.e: In the Minerva Mills case (1980), the Court held the Constitution is founded on the balance between FRs and DPSP; they are like two wheels of a chariot.

questions.q: Which act first recognised the political and administrative functions of the East India Company?
questions.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 recognized, for the first time, the political and administrative functions of the Company.

questions.q: Which article guarantees the ‘Right to Constitutional Remedies’?
questions.e: Article 32 confers the right to remedies for the enforcement of fundamental rights, called the 'soul' of the Constitution by Dr. Ambedkar.

questions.q: The ‘Separation of judiciary from executive’ is provided under which article?
questions.e: Article 50 (a Liberal-Intellectual DPSP) directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

questions.q: Which schedule of the Constitution deals with the division of powers between the Union and the States?
questions.e: The Seventh Schedule contains three lists: List I (Union), List II (State), and List III (Concurrent) for the division of powers.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the 'diwani' rights obtained by the East India Company: 1️⃣ They were granted by the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam in 1765. 2️⃣ They included rights over revenue and civil justice. 3️⃣ These rights covered Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
questions.e: In 1765, after the Battle of Buxar (1764), the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam granted 'diwani' rights (revenue and civil justice) for Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the Company, marking its start as a territorial power.

questions.q: Which of the following acts prohibited the servants of the East India Company from engaging in private trade or accepting bribes from 'natives'?
questions.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 specifically prohibited Company servants from engaging in any private trade or accepting presents or bribes from the 'natives' to ensure better control.

questions.q: With reference to the Board of Control created by Pitt’s India Act of 1784, consider the following statements: 1️⃣ it was established to manage the commercial affairs of the Company. 2️⃣ It was empowered to supervise all operations of the civil and military government. 3️⃣ it reported on the revenues of the British possessions in India.
questions.e: Under Pitt’s India Act of 1784, the Court of Directors managed commercial affairs, while the new Board of Control managed political affairs and supervised civil/military government and revenues.

questions.q: Which act provided that the Commander-in-Chief was not to be a member of the Governor-General’s council unless specifically appointed?
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1793 explicitly provided that the Commander-in-Chief would not be an automatic member of the Governor-General’s council unless he was so appointed.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1813: 1️⃣ It asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company’s territories. 2️⃣ It authorized Local Governments to impose taxes on persons. 3️⃣ It allowed the Company to retain its monopoly over trade in tea and trade with China.
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1813 asserted Crown sovereignty, authorized local taxes, and while opening Indian trade to British merchants, it allowed the Company to keep its tea and China trade monopolies.

questions.q: Under the Charter Act of 1833, the laws made under previous acts were referred to as:
questions.e: The Charter Act of 1833 specified that laws made under previous acts were called 'Regulations', while laws made under this specific act were called 'Acts'.

questions.q: The 'Macaulay Committee', appointed in 1854, was related to which of the following?
questions.e: Following the Charter Act of 1853, which introduced an open competition system for civil servants, the Macaulay Committee (Committee on the Indian Civil Service) was appointed in 1854.

questions.q: Which act changed the designation of the Governor-General of India to that of Viceroy of India?
questions.e: The Government of India Act of 1858 changed the designation of the Governor-General to Viceroy, who acted as the direct representative of the British Crown.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Secretary of State for India established in 1858: 1️⃣ He was a member of the British Cabinet. 2️⃣ He was assisted by a 15-member advisory Council of India. 3️⃣ He was responsible to the Governor-General of India.
questions.e: The Secretary of State was a British Cabinet member responsible to the British Parliament, not the Governor-General. He was assisted by a 15-member advisory Council of India.

questions.q: Which of the following Indians were nominated to the legislative council by Lord Canning in 1862? 1️⃣ Raja of Benaras 2️⃣ Maharaja of Patiala 3️⃣ Sir Dinkar Rao
questions.e: In 1862, acting under the Indian Councils Act of 1861, Viceroy Lord Canning nominated the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala, and Sir Dinkar Rao to his legislative council.

questions.q: Which act empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances during an emergency without the concurrence of the legislative council?
questions.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances during an emergency with a life of six months.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Councils Act of 1892: 1️⃣ It used the word 'election' for the first time in the act. 2️⃣ It increased the number of additional non-official members in councils. 3️⃣ It allowed councils to discuss the budget.
questions.e: The Act of 1892 increased non-official members and allowed budget discussion. While it made limited provision for filling seats, the word 'election' was not used in the Act.

questions.q: Under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, the number of members in the Central legislative council was raised from 16 to:
questions.e: The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 considerably increased the size of the legislative councils, raising the Central legislative council membership from 16 to 60.

questions.q: Who was the first Indian to join the Viceroy’s Executive Council?
questions.e: Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy’s Executive Council when he was appointed as the Law Member under the 1909 Act.

questions.q: Which of the following was a feature of the Government of India Act of 1919? 1️⃣ Classification of subjects into Central and Provincial. 2️⃣ Division of provincial subjects into Transferred and Reserved. 3️⃣ Granting of franchise to all adults regardless of property.
questions.e: The 1919 Act classified subjects and introduced provincial dyarchy. However, it granted franchise to only a limited number of people based on property, tax, or qualifications.

questions.q: The term 'dyarchy' introduced by the 1919 Act is derived from which language?
questions.e: 'Dyarchy' is derived from the Greek word 'di-arche', which means double rule.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Simon Commission: 1️⃣ It was appointed two years before the original schedule. 2️⃣ It recommended the establishment of a federation of British India and princely states. 3️⃣ All parties boycotted it because it had no Indian members.
questions.e: Appointed in 1927 (2 years early), the all-British commission was boycotted. Its 1930 report recommended abolishing dyarchy and establishing a federation.

questions.q: Which of the following were continued as separate electorates under the Communal Award of 1932? 1️⃣ Muslims 2️⃣ Sikhs 3️⃣ Depressed Classes
questions.e: The Communal Award announced by Ramsay MacDonald continued separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, and others, and extended it to the depressed classes.

questions.q: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, residuary powers were given to:
questions.e: The 1935 Act divided powers into three lists, and residuary powers were specifically vested in the Viceroy (Governor-General).

questions.q: In how many provinces was bicameralism introduced by the Government of India Act of 1935?
questions.e: The Act of 1935 introduced bicameral legislatures (legislative council and assembly) in six out of eleven provinces, including Bengal, Bombay, and Madras.

questions.q: Which of the following were created as new provinces by the Government of India Act of 1935?
questions.e: Among its various provisions, the Government of India Act of 1935 created two new provinces: Orissa and Sind.

questions.q: On which day did the Indian Independence Act of 1947 receive Royal Assent?
questions.e: The Indian Independence Bill was introduced on July 4, 1947, and received the Royal Assent on July 18, 1947, coming into force on August 15.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Independence Act of 1947: 1️⃣ It abolished the office of Viceroy. 2️⃣ It provided for a Governor-General for each dominion. 3️⃣ It empowered the Constituent Assemblies to repeal any act of the British Parliament.
questions.e: The Act abolished the Viceroy, established Governors-General appointed by the King, and gave Constituent Assemblies full power to frame constitutions and repeal British acts.

questions.q: Who was the first Prime Minister of independent India?
questions.e: After the British rule ended, Lord Mountbatten swore in Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister of independent India.

questions.q: Who held the portfolio of Education in the First Cabinet of Independent India (1947)?
questions.e: In the first cabinet of 1947, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was the Minister for Education. C. Rajagopalachari held Education in the 1946 Interim Government.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the demand for a Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ M.N. Roy put forward the idea in 1934. 2️⃣ Jawaharlal Nehru declared in 1938 that the constitution must be framed without outside interference. 3️⃣ The Cripps Proposals were rejected by the Muslim League.
questions.e: M.N. Roy first proposed the idea in 1934. Nehru reiterated the demand for an independent assembly in 1938 , and the League rejected the 1942 Cripps draft.

questions.q: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, roughly how many people were to be represented by one seat in the Constituent Assembly?
questions.e: The scheme formulated by the Cabinet Mission Plan allotted seats to provinces and states in proportion to their population, roughly one seat per million people.

questions.q: Which of the following communities were recognized as the 'three principal communities' for seat allocation in 1946?
questions.e: Seats in each British province were divided among three principal communities: Muslims, Sikhs, and General (all others), in proportion to their population.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ It was a fully elected body. 2️⃣ Princely state representatives were nominated by their heads. 3️⃣ Elections for British Indian seats were held in July-August 1946.
questions.e: The assembly was partly elected and partly nominated. Princely states nominated their members , and elections for provincial seats occurred in mid-1946.

questions.q: Who was elected as the permanent Chairman of the Constituent Assembly on December 11, 1946?
questions.e: While Dr. Sinha was the temporary chairman, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent Chairman (President) on December 11, 1946.

questions.q: On which date was the 'Objectives Resolution' unanimously adopted by the Assembly?
questions.e: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the 'Objectives Resolution' on December 13, 1946, and it was unanimously adopted on January 22, 1947.

questions.q: Consider the changes made by the Independence Act of 1947 in the Constituent Assembly: 1️⃣ The Assembly became a fully sovereign body. 2️⃣ It became the first Parliament of free India. 3️⃣ The total strength increased to 389.
questions.e: The Act made the Assembly sovereign and a legislative body (first Parliament). However, the strength decreased to 299 after the withdrawal of Pakistan areas.

questions.q: Who was the Chairman of the Provincial Constitution Committee?
questions.e: Sardar Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee as well as the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities.

questions.q: How many members did the Drafting Committee consist of?
questions.e: The most important committee, the Drafting Committee set up on August 29, 1947, consisted of seven members.

questions.q: Who among the following was the calligrapher of the Indian Constitution?
questions.e: Prem Behari Narain Raizada was the calligrapher who handwrote the original constitution in a flowing italic style.

questions.q: The original Preamble was illuminated and beautified by which artist?
questions.e: While artists from Shantiniketan beautified the original version, Beohar Rammanohar Sinha specifically illuminated and ornamented the original Preamble.

questions.q: The term 'constitution' is derived from the Latin word 'constituere', which means:
questions.e: The term 'constitution' comes from the Latin word 'constituere', meaning 'to establish' or 'to set-up'.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the classification of constitutions: 1️⃣ An evolved constitution is the outcome of a slow evolutionary process. 2️⃣ An enacted constitution is deliberately made by a constituent assembly. 3️⃣ The Indian Constitution is an example of an evolved constitution.
questions.e: Evolved constitutions result from gradual processes , while enacted ones are deliberately created. The Indian and American constitutions are enacted.

questions.q: Who gave the classification of constitutions into 'rigid' and 'flexible'?
questions.e: Lord James Bryce provided the classification based on the method of amendment: rigid (special procedure required) or flexible (amended like ordinary laws).

questions.q: The Constitution of India was described as 'quasi-federal' by:
questions.e: Because the Indian Constitution contains both federal and unitary provisions, K.C. Wheare described it as 'quasi-federal'.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding 'Constitutionalism': 1️⃣ It essentially connotes limited government. 2️⃣ It is the antithesis of arbitrary power. 3️⃣ Despotic rule is a form of constitutionalism.
questions.e: Constitutionalism means limited government and rule of law. It is the opposite of arbitrary, despotic, or totalitarian rule.

questions.q: Which case ruled that the constituent power of Parliament does not enable it to alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
questions.e: In the historic Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that Article 368 does not allow Parliament to alter the constitution's 'basic structure'.

questions.q: Originally (1949), the Constitution of India contained how many Schedules?
questions.e: Originally, the Constitution had a Preamble, 395 Articles (22 Parts), and 8 Schedules. Currently, it has about 470 Articles (25 Parts) and 12 Schedules.

questions.q: Consider the following factors that contributed to the elephantine size of the Indian Constitution: 1️⃣ Geographical factors and diversity. 2️⃣ Influence of the Government of India Act of 1935. 3️⃣ Single Constitution for both Centre and states.
questions.e: Four factors contributed to the size: geography/diversity, the bulky 1935 Act influence, a single constitution for Centre and states, and dominance of legal luminaries .

questions.q: The philosophical part of the Indian Constitution (Fundamental Rights and DPSP) is inspired by:
questions.e: The Fundamental Rights derive inspiration from the American Constitution, and the Directive Principles from the Irish Constitution.

questions.q: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the 'Union of States'?
questions.e: Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States', implying it is not an agreement by states and they have no right to secede.

questions.q: Consider the following features of parliamentary government in India: 1️⃣ Collective responsibility of the executive to the legislature. 2️⃣ Membership of ministers in the legislature. 3️⃣ Presence of only real executives.
questions.e: Indian parliamentary features include nominal and real executives, collective responsibility, and ministerial membership in the legislature .

questions.q: The Right to Property was deleted from the list of Fundamental Rights by which amendment?
questions.e: Originally there were seven Fundamental Rights, but the Right to Property (Article 31) was deleted by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Directive Principles of State Policy: 1️⃣ They are justiciable in nature. 2️⃣ They seek to establish a 'welfare state'. 3️⃣ They are meant for promoting social and economic democracy.
questions.e: Unlike Fundamental Rights, DPSP are non-justiciable. They aim for social/economic democracy and seek to establish a welfare state.

questions.q: The voting age in India was reduced from 21 years to 18 years in 1989 by which amendment?
questions.e: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years, effective in 1989.

questions.q: Which of the following are recognized as 'independent bodies' by the Indian Constitution? 1️⃣ Election Commission 2️⃣ Comptroller and Auditor-General 3️⃣ Union Public Service Commission
questions.e: The Constitution establishes several independent bodies as bulwarks of democracy, including the Election Commission, CAG, and Public Service Commissions .

questions.q: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 gave constitutional recognition to:
questions.e: The 73rd Amendment (1992) recognized Panchayats (rural local governments), while the 74th Amendment recognized Municipalities (urban).

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Preamble: 1️⃣ It contains the summary or essence of the Constitution. 2️⃣ N.A. Palkhivala called it the 'identity card of the Constitution'. 3️⃣ It was amended by the 42nd Amendment Act.
questions.e: The Preamble is the preface or summary of the Constitution. Palkhivala called it an 'identity card' , and it was amended in 1976.

questions.q: Which of the following words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976?
questions.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976) added three new words to the Preamble: Socialist, Secular, and Integrity.

questions.q: The Indian brand of socialism is described as:
questions.e: India follows 'democratic socialism', which holds faith in a 'mixed economy' where public and private sectors co-exist, unlike 'communistic' state socialism.

questions.q: Consider the four devices of direct democracy: 1️⃣ Referendum 2️⃣ Initiative 3️⃣ Recall 4️⃣ Plebiscite. Which are used in Switzerland?
questions.e: Direct democracy, where people exercise power directly, is seen in Switzerland using four devices: Referendum, Initiative, Recall, and Plebiscite.

questions.q: The ideal of 'justice' (social, economic and political) in the Preamble was taken from:
questions.e: The Preamble’s ideal of justice—social, economic, and political—was inspired by the Russian Revolution of 1917.

questions.q: The ideals of 'liberty, equality and fraternity' in the Preamble were taken from:
questions.e: The ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity in the Indian Preamble were adopted from the French Revolution (1789-1799).

questions.q: Which case first raised the question of whether the Preamble can be amended under Article 368?
questions.e: The amendability of the Preamble under Article 368 was first addressed in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the name of the country: 1️⃣ Traditionalists favored 'Bharat'. 2️⃣ Modernists advocated 'India'. 3️⃣ The Constituent Assembly adopted both as 'India, that is, Bharat'.
questions.e: Due to a lack of unanimity, the Constituent Assembly combined both suggestions into Article 1: 'India, that is, Bharat' .

questions.q: Which article relates to the admission or establishment of new states that are NOT part of the Union of India?
questions.e: Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish states not already part of India. Article 3 deals with changes to existing constituent states.

questions.q: The 100th Constitutional Amendment Act (2015) was related to:
questions.e: The 100th Amendment (2015) was enacted to give effect to the transfer of 111 enclaves to Bangladesh and the acquisition of 51 enclaves by India.

questions.q: Hyderabad was integrated into the Indian Union by means of:
questions.e: While most joined freely, Hyderabad was integrated via police action, Junagarh via referendum, and Kashmir via the Instrument of Accession.

questions.q: The 1950 Constitution classified states into how many categories?
questions.e: In 1950, the Constitution had a four-fold classification: Part A, Part B, Part C states, and Part D territories.

questions.q: The JVP Committee (1948) included which of the following members? 1️⃣ Jawaharlal Nehru 2️⃣ Vallahbhai Patel 3️⃣ Pattabhi Sitaramayya
questions.e: The Linguistic Provinces Committee, known as the JVP Committee after its members Nehru, Patel, and Sitaramayya, rejected language as the basis for states in 1949.

questions.q: On the recommendation of which commission were 14 states and 6 union territories created on November 1, 1956?
questions.e: The States Reorganisation Commission under Fazl Ali led to the States Reorganisation Act (1956), creating 14 states and 6 UTs.

questions.q: Which of the following territories was governed by the Portuguese until its liberation in 1954?
questions.e: Dadra and Nagar Haveli was ruled by the Portuguese until 1954, then administered by an administrator until becoming a UT in 1961.

questions.q: The state of Nagaland was formed in 1963 by taking the Naga Hills and Tuensang area out of:
questions.e: In 1963, Nagaland became the 16th state by taking territories out of the state of Assam.

questions.q: Which state was created in 2014 as the 29th state of the Indian Union?
questions.e: Telangana came into existence in 2014 as the 29th state, carved out of the territories of Andhra Pradesh.

questions.q: Consider the following changes of names: 1️⃣ Madras renamed Tamil Nadu (1969). 2️⃣ Mysore renamed Karnataka (1973). 3️⃣ Orissa renamed Odisha (2011).
questions.e: Several states changed names: Madras in 1969 , Mysore and Laccadive Islands in 1973 , and Orissa in 2011.

questions.q: The Constitution confers which of the following rights ONly on citizens?  1️⃣ Right to vote in elections 2️⃣ Right to contest for Parliament 3️⃣ Eligibility for the office of President
questions.e: Citizens enjoy specific privileges denied to aliens, including voting, contesting elections, and eligibility for high offices like President.

questions.q: In which country is only a 'citizen by birth' (not naturalized) eligible for the office of President?
questions.e: In India, both citizens by birth and naturalized citizens are eligible for the Presidency, while in the USA, only citizens by birth are eligible.

questions.q: Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution deal with:
questions.e: Part II of the Constitution, consisting of Articles 5 to 11, deals with citizenship matters.

questions.q: Consider the categories of persons who became Indian citizens on January 26, 1950: 1️⃣ Persons domiciled in India. 2️⃣ Persons migrated from Pakistan. 3️⃣ Persons of Indian origin residing outside India.
questions.e: The Constitution identified four categories at its commencement: those domiciled in India, migrants from Pakistan, those who returned from Pakistan, and overseas Indians.

questions.q: The Citizenship Act (1955) prescribes how many ways of acquiring citizenship?
questions.e: The Act prescribes five ways: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory.

questions.q: A minor child of an Indian citizen renouncing their citizenship:
questions.e: When an Indian citizen renounces their citizenship, every minor child of that person also loses Indian citizenship.

questions.q: Part III of the Constitution is described as the:
questions.e: Part III, containing Fundamental Rights, is rightly described as the Magna Carta of India.

questions.q: Which of the following fundamental rights is available to BOTH citizens and foreigners (except enemy aliens)?
o: Equality of opportunity in public employment
questions.e: Article 14 (Equality before law) is available to both, while Articles 16, 19, and 29 are available only to citizens .

questions.q: The term 'State' under Article 12 includes:  1️⃣ Government and Parliament of India 2️⃣ All local authorities like municipalities 3️⃣ Statutory authorities like LIC and ONGC
questions.e: Article 12 defines 'State' broadly to include the Union/State governments, local bodies, and other statutory or non-statutory authorities .

questions.q: The concept of 'equality before law' is of which origin?
questions.e: 'Equality before law' is of British origin, while 'equal protection of laws' comes from the American Constitution.

questions.q: Which article prohibits discrimination on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth?
questions.e: Article 15 provides that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on these five specific grounds.

questions.q: The 'creamy layer' among OBCs includes children of:  1️⃣ Persons holding constitutional posts 2️⃣ Group 'A' / Class I Officers 3️⃣ Persons in the rank of colonel and above in the Army
questions.e: Benefit of reservation is excluded for the 'creamy layer', which includes children of high constitutional officers, senior civil servants, and high-ranking military officers .

questions.q: Which case is also known as the 'Mandal case'?
questions.e: The Indra Sawhney vs. Union of India (1992) case is popularly known as the Mandal case.

questions.q: The 77th Amendment Act (1995) was enacted to:
o: Provide reservation in promotions for SCs and STs
questions.e: This amendment empowered the State to provide reservation in promotions for SCs and STs not adequately represented in services.

questions.q: The total number of Padma Awards to be given in a year (excluding posthumous and foreign) should not exceed:
questions.e: Government rules restrict the total number of Padma Awards in a year to a maximum of 120.

questions.q: Consider the rights guaranteed by Article 19: 1️⃣ Freedom of speech 2️⃣ Freedom of assembly 3️⃣ Freedom to form co-operative societies. Which were added by the 97th Amendment?
questions.e: The provision for "co-operative societies" in Article 19(1)(c) was added by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011.

questions.q: The protection against 'double jeopardy' means:
o: No person shall be punished for the same offence more than once.
No person can be compelled to be a witness against himself.
No person shall be convicted of an ex-post-facto law.
No person can be arrested without a warrant.
questions.e: Article 20(b) provides for 'no double jeopardy', meaning no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court declare the 'Right to Privacy' as an integral part of Article 21?
questions.e: In K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India (2017), the Court declared the Right to Privacy as a part of the protection of life and personal liberty under Article 21.

questions.q: The 'Right to Education' (Article 21A) provides for free and compulsory education to children of which age group?
questions.e: Article 21A, added in 2002, requires the State to provide free and compulsory elementary education to children aged six to fourteen.

questions.q: Punitive detention is intended to:
o: Prevent a person from committing a crime in the future.
Punish a person for an offence committed by him after trial.
Restrain an individual based on suspicion.
questions.e: Punitive detention is for punishment after trial and conviction, while preventive detention is a precautionary measure based on suspicion .

questions.q: The maximum period for which a person can be detained under a preventive detention law without an advisory board's opinion is:
questions.e: Under Article 22, detention cannot exceed three months unless an advisory board reports sufficient cause. Though the 44th Amendment sought to reduce this, the 3-month period still continues.

questions.q: 'Begar', prohibited under Article 23, refers to:
questions.e: 'Begar' was a system where local landlords forced tenants to render services without any payment, which is now prohibited.

questions.q: Which act renamed the 'Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955'?
o: Scheduled Castes Prevention of Atrocities Act
questions.e: In 1976, the 1955 Act was amended and renamed as the Protection of Civil Rights Act to make penal provisions more stringent.

questions.q: Consider the religious rights under Article 25: 1️⃣ Freedom of conscience 2️⃣ Right to profess 3️⃣ Right to forcibly convert others.
questions.e: Article 25 covers conscience, profession, practice, and propagation, but it does NOT include a right to convert another person, as forcible conversions impinge on others' freedom of conscience .

questions.q: Which of the following are included in the definition of 'Hindus' for the purpose of Article 25?
questions.e: Explanation II of Article 25 states that references to Hindus shall be construed as including persons professing the Sikh, Jaina, and Buddhist religions.

questions.q: Which article prohibits religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds?
questions.e: Under Article 28, religious instruction is completely prohibited in institutions maintained entirely by the State.

questions.q: The term 'minority' is defined in which part of the Constitution?
questions.e: Although Articles 29 and 30 provide rights to religious and linguistic minorities, the term 'minority' has not been defined anywhere in the Constitution.

questions.q: Who called Article 32 the 'soul of the Constitution'?
questions.e: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) as the most important article—the very soul and heart of the Constitution.

questions.q: The 'prerogative writs' in India are borrowed from:
questions.e: The writs (habeas corpus, etc.) are borrowed from English law, where they were issued by the King as the 'fountain of justice'.

questions.q: Which writ literally means 'we command'?
questions.e: Mandamus is a command issued by the court to a public official to perform failed or refused official duties.

questions.q: The writ of Prohibition is issued to:
o: Enquire into legality of claim to office.
questions.e: Unlike Mandamus (directs activity), Prohibition directs inactivity by preventing a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction.

questions.q: Which article empowers Parliament to restrict the fundamental rights of members of the armed forces?
questions.e: Article 33 allows Parliament (and not state legislatures) to limit FRs for armed forces, police, and intelligence agencies to ensure discipline .

questions.q: Martial law differs from National Emergency because:
o: Martial law has specific provisions in the Constitution.
Martial law suspends ordinary law courts.
National Emergency affects only Fundamental Rights.
National Emergency is imposed only in specific areas.
questions.e: Martial law suspends the government and ordinary courts, while they continue during a National Emergency.

questions.q: Which amendment abolished the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right?
questions.e: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, making the right to property a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A .

questions.q: Article 31C was inserted by which amendment?
questions.e: Article 31C, which saves laws giving effect to certain directive principles from being challenged as violative of Articles 14 or 19, was inserted by the 25th Amendment Act of 1971.

questions.q: Directive Principles resemble the 'Instrument of Instructions' found in which document?
questions.e: Dr. Ambedkar noted that DPSP are like the instructions issued to Governors under the 1935 Act.

questions.q: Which article of the Constitution declares that DPSP are 'fundamental in the governance of the country'?
questions.e: Article 37 states that while DPSP are non-justiciable, they are fundamental in governance and the State has a duty to apply them in making laws.

questions.q: Match the following DPSP categories: 1️⃣ Socialistic: Equal pay for equal work 2️⃣ Gandhian: Promote cottage industries 3️⃣ Liberal-Intellectual: Uniform Civil Code
o: None of the pairs are correctly matched
Only two pairs are correctly matched
All three pairs are correctly matched
Only one pair is correctly matched
questions.e: DPSP are classified into socialistic (Article 39) , Gandhian (Article 43) , and liberal-intellectual (Article 44).

questions.q: The 'Minerva Mills case' (1980) declared which extension of Article 31C as unconstitutional?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment tried to protect laws implementing ANY directive principle, but the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills declared this extension invalid.

questions.q: The 'Swaran Singh Committee' was set up during the operation of:
questions.e: The Congress Party set up the committee in 1976 to recommend fundamental duties during the internal emergency.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'civic duty' among the Fundamental Duties?
o: Cherishing noble ideals of freedom struggle.
questions.e: Respecting the Flag and Anthem are categorized as civic duties, while cherishing freedom struggle ideals is a moral duty.

questions.q: The 'Verma Committee' (1999) relates to:
questions.e: The Verma Committee identified existing legal provisions for implementing some Fundamental Duties.

questions.q: The 'Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972' helps implement which fundamental duty?
questions.e: This act prohibits trade in rare species, serving to implement the duty to protect the natural environment.

questions.q: Which act provides for punishments for encouraging enmity between different sections on grounds of language or race?
questions.e: Various criminal laws in force, including the IPC, provide punishments for acts that encourage communal or racial enmity.

questions.q: The Planning Commission, established in 1950, was replaced in 2015 by:
questions.e: Successive Five Year Plans implemented DPSP until 2015, when the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog .

questions.q: Which of the following is a right found OUTSIDE Part III of the Constitution?  1️⃣ Right to property (300-A) 2️⃣ Freedom of trade and commerce (301) 3️⃣ Adult suffrage (326)
questions.e: These are constitutional/legal rights equally justiciable but different from FRs because they cannot be enforced directly via Article 32 .

questions.q: The 86th Amendment Act of 2002 added an 11th Fundamental Duty regarding:
questions.e: The 86th Amendment added the duty for parents/guardians to provide educational opportunities to their children aged 6-14.

questions.q: Which article empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
questions.e: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for FR enforcement; the court can issue writs like habeas corpus and mandamus .

questions.q: The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 is:
o: Exactly the same as the Supreme Court.
questions.e: High Courts can issue writs for FRs AND 'any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights), making their scope wider than the SC's .

questions.q: Which article prohibits the employment of children below 14 years in factories or mines?
questions.e: Article 24 forbids hazardous child labor but does not prohibit employment in harmless or innocent work.

questions.q: In the 'Gopalan case' (1950), the Supreme Court held that Article 21 protects only against:
questions.e: Initially, the SC took a narrow view that protection was available only against arbitrary executive action, not legislative action.

questions.q: 'Ex-post-facto laws' are prohibited by Article 20, but this limitation applies only to:
questions.e: Retrospective penalties are prohibited for criminal laws, but civil liabilities or taxes can be imposed retrospectively.

questions.q: Which article guarantees freedom to manage religious affairs to every denomination?
questions.e: While Article 25 protects individual rights, Article 26 protects the collective freedom of religious denominations.

questions.q: Article 29 protects the rights of:
o: Only citizens residing in rural areas.
questions.e: Although commonly associated with minorities, the SC held that the term 'section of citizens' includes both minorities and the majority.

questions.q: Minority educational institutions that seek NEITHER recognition NOR aid from the State:
o: Are subject to syllabus prescription by the State.
Are free to administer their affairs subject to general laws.
Must follow State rules for employment of staff.
questions.e: The third type of minority institution is free to administer itself but must follow general laws like contract, labor, and tax law.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'Socialistic Principle' in the DPSP?  1️⃣ Minimize inequalities in income 2️⃣ Free legal aid to the poor 3️⃣ Early childhood care
questions.e: Minimizing inequalities (Article 38) and free legal aid (39A) are socialistic. Early childhood care (Article 45) is a liberal-intellectual principle.

questions.q: The 'Swaran Singh Committee' suggested how many Fundamental Duties?
questions.e: The committee suggested eight duties, but the 42nd Amendment eventually included ten.

questions.q: Which fundamental duty was added to protect the 'dignity of women'?
o: To renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
questions.e: Article 51A(e) makes it a duty to promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to women.

questions.q: Laws made under Article 3 for the formation of new states are passed by:
o: Simple majority and ordinary legislative process.
questions.e: Article 4 declares that laws for Admission (Art 2) or Formation (Art 3) of states are NOT considered constitutional amendments under Article 368.

questions.q: The 'Instrument of Accession' was the method used to integrate:
questions.e: Hyderabad was integrated by police action, Junagarh by referendum, and Kashmir by signing the Instrument of Accession.

questions.q: Which UT was redesignated as the 'National Capital Territory of Delhi' in 1992?
questions.e: The 69th Amendment Act of 1991 redesignated Delhi as the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

questions.q: 'Friendly aliens' are subjects of countries that:
questions.e: Aliens are divided into friendly (cordial relations) or enemy (at war). Enemy aliens have fewer rights, such as no protection under Article 22 .

questions.q: The 'Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957' authorized residential qualifications for which states?
o: Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur and Tripura
questions.e: This Act, which mostly expired in 1974, originally applied to these four states; currently, only AP and Telangana have such provisions via Article 371-D.

questions.q: To acquire citizenship by 'Naturalisation', a person must have an adequate knowledge of a language specified in:
questions.e: One qualification for naturalisation is adequate knowledge of one of the 22 languages recognized in the Eighth Schedule.

questions.q: 'Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholders' are NOT entitled to:  1️⃣ Right to vote 2️⃣ Eligibility for election as President 3️⃣ Appointment as a SC Judge
questions.e: OCI cardholders are foreign nationals and are denied several rights available to Indian citizens, including voting and holding high constitutional offices .

questions.q: The 'Ninth Schedule' was added to the Constitution by which amendment?
questions.e: The First Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from judicial review.

questions.q: Which writ is issued to quash the order passed by a lower court?
questions.e: Certiorari is issued on grounds of excess or lack of jurisdiction to quash an order already passed by a lower tribunal .

questions.q: Article 31A saves laws related to:
questions.e: Article 31A saves five categories of laws, primarily related to land reforms and industry, from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 .

questions.q: In the 'Waman Rao case' (1980), the SC held that acts in the Ninth Schedule are valid only if they:
o: Do not damage the basic structure.
questions.e: The Court clarified that laws added after April 24, 1973, are subject to judicial review if they damage the Constitution's basic structure.

questions.q: Which DPSP directs the state to 'separate the judiciary from the executive'?
questions.e: Article 50 requires the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

questions.q: 'Uniform Civil Code for the citizens' is mentioned under:
questions.e: Article 44, a Liberal-Intellectual Principle, directs the State to endeavor to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens.

questions.q: Which case held that 'political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy'?
questions.e: Dr. Ambedkar stressed this in his concluding speech, defining social democracy as a way of life recognizing liberty, equality, and fraternity.

questions.q: 'Distributive justice' denotes a combination of:
questions.e: The combination of social justice (equal treatment) and economic justice (eliminating inequalities) results in distributive justice .

questions.q: Sovereignty of Parliament is associated with which system?
questions.e: Parliamentary sovereignty is a British concept, while judicial supremacy is associated with the American Supreme Court.

questions.q: 'Procedure established by Law' is found in Article 21, while 'Due process of Law' is a feature of:
questions.e: Article 21 uses the Japanese-inspired 'procedure established by law', which is narrower than the American 'due process of law'.

questions.q: Which body audits the accounts of both Central and state governments?
questions.e: The CAG acts as the guardian of the public purse and audits all government expenditure.

questions.q: A 'National Emergency' under Article 352 can be declared on the grounds of:
o: War, external aggression or armed rebellion
questions.e: Proclamation of Emergency is allowed for war, aggression, or armed rebellion (which replaced 'internal disturbance' in 1978).

questions.q: The 97th Amendment Act of 2011 gave constitutional status to:
questions.e: This amendment made forming co-operatives a Fundamental Right and added a new DPSP and Part IX-B to the Constitution .

questions.q: Which critic called the Indian Constitution a 'lawyer's paradise'?
questions.e: Due to its legalistic language and complicated phraseology, Ivor Jennings and other critics described the constitution as a paradise for lawyers .

questions.q: The 'Magna Carta', the first written document on Fundamental Rights, was issued in:
questions.e: King John of England issued the Magna Carta in 1215 under pressure from barons; it is the historical ancestor of modern Fundamental Rights.
